content: Scheelite is a mineral composed of calcium tungstate, with the chemical formula CaWO₄. It serves as a significant ore for tungsten extraction. Well-formed crystals of scheelite are highly valued by collectors and, when free of imperfections, are occasionally cut into gemstones. Synthetic scheelite has been produced using the Czochralski process, and the resulting material can be used as a diamond simulant, a scintillator, or a solid-state lasing medium. Scheelite crystallizes in the tetragonal crystal system, often forming dipyramidal pseudo-octahedra. Its color varies and includes golden yellow, brownish-green to dark brown, pinkish to reddish-gray, and even colorless varieties. The mineral ranges from translucent to transparent, with crystal faces exhibiting a vitreous to adamantine luster. It has distinct cleavage, and its fracture can be subconchoidal to uneven. In addition to pseudo-octahedral forms, scheelite may also appear in columnar, granular, tabular, or massive habits. Twinning is commonly observed, and crystal faces may display striations. The mineral has a white streak and is brittle. Its relatively high refractive index and dispersion contribute to its notable luster and fire, which can approach that of diamond. However, due to its low hardness, cut scheelite is best appreciated as unset collector's pieces rather than in jewelry. Scheelite is particularly prized for its fluorescent properties. Under shortwave ultraviolet light, it emits a bright sky-blue glow. Trace impurities of molybdenum can sometimes cause a green fluorescence. This fluorescence has made scheelite a valuable tool for prospectors, who often search for deposits at night using ultraviolet lamps. Many old mines have been reopened after ultraviolet examination revealed remaining ore deposits. The structure of scheelite consists of isolated tetrahedra that form non-touching one-dimensional chains aligned in two distinct directions. Tungsten deposits, including scheelite, are typically formed under high-temperature and high-pressure conditions, with most deposits occurring between 200°C and 500°C and at pressures ranging from 200 to 1,500 bars. Scheelite is often grayish-white in color, with yellowish, brownish, or translucent variations. Its streak is white, and it has a greasy luster, which helps distinguish it from other minerals. Miners frequently use ultraviolet light to identify scheelite due to its characteristic bright blue fluorescence. This property has been instrumental in locating scheelite deposits, and many mines have been reexamined and reopened based on this fluorescence. Tungsten, extracted from scheelite, can combine with carbon to form tungsten carbide, one of the hardest known substances aside from diamond. Tungsten carbide is widely used in abrasive wheels and cutting tools, with demand steadily increasing. Although synthetic scheelite is now rarely used as a diamond imitation—having been surpassed by more convincing materials like cubic zirconia and moissanite—it is occasionally marketed as natural scheelite, potentially deceiving collectors into paying high prices. Gemologists distinguish natural scheelite from synthetic material primarily through microscopic examination. Natural scheelite typically contains internal growth features and inclusions, while synthetic scheelite is usually very clean. Synthetic scheelite may also exhibit artificial curved striae and clouds of minute gas bubbles. Additionally, the visible absorption spectrum of scheelite, observed with a hand-held spectroscope, can aid in differentiation. Most natural stones display faint absorption lines in the yellow region (~585 nm) due to trace impurities of praseodymium and neodymium, whereas synthetic scheelite often lacks this spectrum. Some synthetic materials may be doped with rare earth elements like neodymium, but their spectra differ from those of natural stones. The Swedish chemist and apothecary Carl Wilhelm Scheele first identified tungstic oxide in scheelite in 1781. Born in Stralsund, Pomerania, Scheele studied chemistry and later opened a pharmacy where he conducted groundbreaking research. He made numerous discoveries, including the identification of lactic acid as the source of sour milk's acidity. His work on the composition of the mineral tungsten, later named scheelite in his honor, led to the isolation of tungstic acid, a discovery for which he is also renowned.
